**[Section 1: Purpose and Scope of This Playbook]{.underline}**

This playbook sets forth Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.\'s (\"**Pinnacle**\" or the \"**Company**\") mandatory, preferred, and fallback negotiation positions for Data Processing Agreements (\"**DPAs**\") with third-party vendors and service providers that process personal data on Pinnacle\'s behalf. The purpose of this document is to ensure consistency, regulatory compliance, and efficient negotiation across all vendor DPA engagements by providing Pinnacle\'s legal team and authorized negotiators with clear, tiered guidance on acceptable contractual terms.

Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation operating as a US-based digital health platform company. The Company provides cloud-based electronic health records management, telehealth facilitation, patient engagement tools, and healthcare analytics services to healthcare providers across the United States.

Pinnacle acts as a **HIPAA Covered Entity** for certain data flows involving Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") of approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts**. These data flows are central to Pinnacle\'s core service offerings and are implicated in the majority of vendor engagements involving clinical and patient-facing data processing activities.

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents**, triggering obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"). Given the significant volume of California resident data processed by Pinnacle and its vendors, CCPA/CPRA compliance is a primary concern in all vendor DPA negotiations involving consumer-facing data.

Pinnacle is expanding into the European Union with a target launch date of **September 1, 2025**. The Company\'s EU operations will be conducted through its wholly owned subsidiary, **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**, registered in the Netherlands at Herengracht 450, 1017 CA Amsterdam. Pinnacle EU B.V. will act as Controller under the General Data Protection Regulation (\"**GDPR**\") for an estimated **150,000 projected EU patients** and approximately **320 EU healthcare provider contacts** in Year 1. This EU expansion introduces GDPR obligations that intersect with and complement Pinnacle\'s existing US data protection requirements.
This playbook addresses the following regulatory regimes and their implications for vendor DPA negotiations:
> • **HIPAA/HITECH**, including Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") requirements;
> • **CCPA/CPRA**, including Service Provider qualification and certification requirements;
> • **GDPR**, including Article 28 processor requirements and cross-border data transfer mechanisms; and
> • **Pinnacle\'s internal data governance standards**, which in certain areas exceed the minimum requirements of applicable law.

**Important Note:** This playbook does NOT replace the requirement for outside counsel review of DPAs involving novel or high-risk processing activities. Negotiators must escalate to **Rachel Osterfeld** at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP for matters involving cross-border transfers to jurisdictions without adequacy decisions, novel HIPAA scenarios (including first-of-kind technology deployments involving PHI), regulatory enforcement actions or investigations, or any matter where the vendor\'s proposed terms deviate materially from the positions set forth herein and the applicable fallback position is inadequate to protect Pinnacle\'s interests.
**[Section 2: Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s vendor DPA negotiations must account for three primary regulatory regimes, each of which imposes distinct and, in some cases, overlapping requirements on the contractual relationship between Pinnacle and its data processing vendors. Understanding the interplay among these regimes is essential for effective negotiation. This Section provides a summary overview; detailed negotiation positions for each regime are set forth in the Sections that follow.

The three regimes are: (1) the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009 (\"**HIPAA/HITECH**\"); (2) the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"); and (3) the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (\"**GDPR**\"). Each regime imposes its own definitions, obligations, and enforcement mechanisms, and each requires specific contractual provisions in vendor agreements. Where a vendor processes data subject to multiple regimes (which is increasingly common in Pinnacle\'s vendor portfolio), the DPA must address all applicable requirements, and the most restrictive standard generally governs.

Negotiators should be aware that many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted primarily with GDPR in mind and may fail to address HIPAA or CCPA/CPRA requirements. It is the negotiator\'s responsibility to identify these gaps and require the addition of all necessary provisions before execution.
**[2.1 HIPAA / HITECH]{.underline}**

Pinnacle is a **Covered Entity** under HIPAA as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103. Any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") on Pinnacle\'s behalf qualifies as a **Business Associate** under 45 CFR § 160.103 and is subject to the full range of HIPAA and HITECH requirements applicable to Business Associates.

All DPAs with Business Associates **MUST** incorporate a **Business Associate Agreement** (\"**BAA**\"), either as an integrated section within the DPA body or as a standalone exhibit appended to and expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. This requirement is non-negotiable and derives from the mandatory contractual provisions set forth in **45 CFR § 164.502(e)** and **45 CFR § 164.504(e)**.
A compliant BAA must include, at a minimum, the following elements:
1\. **Definitions** of PHI, Covered Entity, and Business Associate consistent with HIPAA regulatory definitions;

2\. **Permitted uses and disclosures** of PHI, limited to those necessary to perform services under the DPA and Master Services Agreement (\"MSA\"), and consistent with the minimum necessary standard;

3\. **Minimum necessary standard** compliance (45 CFR § 164.502(b)), requiring the vendor to limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the processing;
4\. **Workforce training requirements**, obligating the vendor to train all workforce members with access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements;

5\. **Breach notification obligations**, requiring prompt notification to Pinnacle, and supporting Pinnacle\'s obligations to notify affected individuals and the Department of Health and Human Services (\"**HHS**\") in accordance with the HITECH Act breach notification provisions;

6\. **HIPAA Security Rule safeguard categories**, requiring the vendor to implement and maintain reasonable and appropriate administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312);

7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));

8\. **Record retention of six (6) years** per 45 CFR § 164.530(j), covering all HIPAA-required documentation including the BAA itself, policies and procedures, training records, and incident records; and

9\. **Return or destruction of PHI at termination**, with exceptions where return or destruction is infeasible, in which case the protections of the BAA must extend to all retained PHI for as long as it is maintained.

Negotiators should be particularly alert to vendor DPA templates that reference GDPR Article 28 processor requirements but omit any reference to HIPAA. Where a vendor will process PHI, the absence of a BAA renders the DPA non-compliant regardless of how robust the GDPR provisions may be.
**[2.2 CCPA / CPRA]{.underline}**

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient-facing platform, provider network, and marketing and analytics activities. This volume substantially exceeds the CCPA/CPRA applicability thresholds and places Pinnacle squarely within the statute\'s scope as a \"**Business**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d).

Vendors that process California personal information on Pinnacle\'s behalf must qualify as \"**Service Providers**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag). The Service Provider designation is not automatic; it requires specific contractual provisions that restrict the vendor\'s use, retention, and disclosure of personal information received from Pinnacle. Without these contractual provisions, a vendor may be deemed a \"third party\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which could expose Pinnacle to claims that it has \"sold\" or \"shared\" personal information in violation of the statute.
DPAs with vendors processing California personal information must include the following provisions, which are treated as **must-have** requirements in all negotiations:
> • A **contractual prohibition** on selling or sharing personal information, as those terms are defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad) (\"sale\") and § 1798.140(ah) (\"share\");

> • A **prohibition on combining** personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information received from any other person or entity, or collected from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA;

> • A **prohibition on using** personal information for any purpose other than the specific business purpose set forth in the DPA or MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement;
> • A **certification** in which the vendor expressly certifies that it understands these restrictions and will comply with them, as required under CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d).

These provisions are mandatory for all vendors with access to California resident data. A vendor DPA that omits these provisions, or that contains language inconsistent with the Service Provider classification, must be redlined before execution. Detailed negotiation positions for CCPA/CPRA terms are set forth in Section 7 of this playbook.
**[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**

Upon Pinnacle\'s EU expansion, which is scheduled for **September 1, 2025**, Pinnacle (acting through its subsidiary **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**) will function as **Controller** under the GDPR for the processing of personal data of EU/EEA data subjects. Vendor DPAs must comply with **GDPR Article 28** processor requirements, which mandate a written contract between the controller and processor that sets forth the subject-matter and duration of processing, the nature and purpose of processing, the types of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.
Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
> • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;
> • **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** certification, where the receiving entity is certified and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities; and
> • **Binding Corporate Rules**, where applicable and approved by the competent supervisory authority.

GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.
**[Section 3: Definitions --- Required Contractual Definitions]{.underline}**

Every Pinnacle DPA must include clearly defined terms organized by regulatory regime. The inclusion of complete and accurate definitions is essential to ensuring that the DPA\'s operative provisions are enforceable and that each party\'s obligations are unambiguous. This Section sets forth the required defined terms and Pinnacle\'s negotiation positions regarding their inclusion.
**[3.1 Required Defined Terms by Regulatory Regime]{.underline}**
**GDPR Definitions (per Article 4)**
The following terms must be defined consistently with GDPR Article 4:
> • **Personal Data** (Art. 4(1))
> • **Processing** (Art. 4(2))
> • **Controller** (Art. 4(7))
> • **Processor** (Art. 4(8))
> • **Data Subject** (Art. 4(1))
> • **Personal Data Breach** (Art. 4(12))
> • **Supervisory Authority** (Art. 4(21))
**HIPAA Definitions (per 45 CFR § 160.103 and the HITECH Act)**
The following terms must be defined consistently with HIPAA regulatory definitions:
> • **Protected Health Information (PHI)** (45 CFR § 160.103)
> • **Electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI)** (45 CFR § 160.103)
> • **Covered Entity** (45 CFR § 160.103)
> • **Business Associate** (45 CFR § 160.103)
> • **Business Associate Agreement** (45 CFR § 164.504(e))
> • **Breach** (as defined under the HITECH Act, 42 U.S.C. § 17921(1))
> • **Unsecured PHI** (45 CFR § 164.402)
**CCPA/CPRA Definitions (per Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140)**
The following terms must be defined consistently with the CCPA/CPRA statutory definitions:
> • **Personal Information** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(v))
> • **Service Provider** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag))
> • **Business** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d))
> • **Business Purpose** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(e))
> • **Sale** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad))
> • **Share** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ah))
> • **Consumer** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(i))
**[3.2 Negotiation Positions for Definitions]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA must include all three sets of definitions where the vendor processes data subject to multiple regulatory regimes. Many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted to address GDPR only and will include GDPR definitions but omit HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA definitions entirely. Where this is the case, the negotiator must require the addition of both the HIPAA definitions and the CCPA/CPRA definitions before the DPA is finalized. A DPA that covers PHI but lacks the defined term \"Protected Health Information\" creates ambiguity regarding the scope of the vendor\'s obligations and may be insufficient to satisfy the BAA requirements of 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Similarly, a DPA that covers California personal information but lacks the defined terms \"Service Provider,\" \"Sale,\" and \"Share\" may fail to establish the vendor\'s qualification as a Service Provider under the CCPA/CPRA, with potentially significant regulatory consequences for Pinnacle.

**Nice-to-have:** A single, integrated definitions section within the DPA body, rather than separate definitions scattered across the DPA, BAA exhibit, and CCPA addendum. An integrated definitions section reduces the risk of inconsistent or conflicting definitions and simplifies interpretation and enforcement.

**Fallback:** HIPAA definitions may be incorporated by reference to the BAA exhibit, and CCPA/CPRA definitions may be incorporated by reference to a CCPA/CPRA Addendum, so long as both the BAA exhibit and the CCPA/CPRA Addendum are appended to and expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should confirm that the cross-references are accurate and that the defined terms in the exhibit or addendum are consistent with the terms used in the DPA body.
**[Section 4: HIPAA Business Associate Agreement Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). Failure to execute a compliant BAA with a vendor that processes PHI exposes Pinnacle to enforcement action by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (\"**OCR**\"), including civil monetary penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year (as adjusted for inflation). Equally important, the absence of a BAA means that any disclosure of PHI to the vendor may itself constitute a HIPAA violation.

ALL vendors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on Pinnacle\'s behalf must execute a BAA. There are no exceptions to this requirement. This Section sets forth the must-have, nice-to-have, and fallback positions for BAA terms, as well as non-negotiable red lines.
**[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.
The BAA must specify, at a minimum, the following terms:

> **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. The BAA should enumerate the specific permitted purposes and should include a catch-all restriction providing that any use or disclosure not expressly authorized is prohibited.

> **(b) Minimum Necessary Standard.** The BAA must require vendor compliance with the \"minimum necessary\" standard set forth in 45 CFR § 164.502(b). Vendor must limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of each use, disclosure, or request. Vendor must implement policies and procedures to identify the workforce members who need access to PHI and to limit each such workforce member\'s access to the minimum PHI necessary for that person\'s role.

> **(c) Workforce Training.** Vendor must train all workforce members who have access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements. Training must be provided upon hiring and at least annually thereafter. Vendor must maintain documentation of training completion and make such documentation available to Pinnacle upon reasonable request.
> **(d) HIPAA Security Rule Safeguards.** Vendor must implement and maintain safeguards consistent with the three categories of the HIPAA Security Rule:

> \(i\) **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including risk analysis and risk management, security management processes, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, and evaluation;
> \(ii\) **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use and security, and device and media controls; and
> \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.

> **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). This flow-down obligation must be contractually documented between vendor and each such subcontractor before PHI is made available to the subcontractor.
> **(f) Breach Notification.** The BAA must include breach notification obligations consistent with the HITECH Act requirements, as described in detail in Section 5 of this playbook.

> **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). This includes the BAA itself, policies and procedures relating to the protection of PHI, workforce training records, incident response records, and risk assessment documentation.

> **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.

**Nice-to-have:** The BAA should be integrated directly into the DPA body rather than attached as a separate exhibit. Integration reduces the risk of gaps in coverage that can arise when the DPA and BAA are separate documents with potentially inconsistent terms, different effective dates, or different amendment procedures. An integrated BAA also simplifies contract management and ensures that the BAA\'s security and audit provisions are consistent with the corresponding DPA provisions.

**Fallback:** A standalone BAA exhibit is acceptable if the following conditions are met: (i) the BAA exhibit is expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference; (ii) the BAA cross-references the DPA\'s security, audit, and breach notification provisions to ensure consistency; (iii) the BAA is executed simultaneously with the DPA and by the same authorized signatories; and (iv) the BAA includes a provision stating that, in the event of a conflict between the BAA and the DPA, the more protective provision governs with respect to the handling of PHI.
**[4.2 BAA Negotiation Red Lines]{.underline}**

Pinnacle will **NOT** execute a DPA without a conforming BAA where the vendor processes PHI. This is a **non-negotiable requirement** driven by federal law. No business justification, no vendor relationship importance, and no time pressure overrides this requirement.

If a vendor refuses to execute a BAA, or if a vendor\'s proposed BAA is materially deficient and the vendor refuses to negotiate acceptable terms, the negotiator must **escalate immediately** to Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel, and to Rachel Osterfeld at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP. Under no circumstances should a negotiator proceed with DPA execution in the absence of a conforming BAA.

For context, Pinnacle currently has approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts** whose PHI may be processed by vendors in the course of providing services to Pinnacle. The regulatory and reputational exposure associated with unauthorized disclosure of this PHI is substantial. OCR enforcement actions in recent years have resulted in settlements and penalties ranging from \$100,000 to over \$16 million for HIPAA violations involving inadequate BAA protections.

Negotiators should also be aware that some vendors may propose a \"HIPAA addendum\" or \"healthcare data supplement\" that purports to address HIPAA requirements but does not contain all of the mandatory BAA provisions listed in Section 4.1 above. Such documents must be carefully reviewed against the checklist in Section 4.1, and any missing provisions must be added before execution.
**[Section 5: Breach Notification]{.underline}**

Breach notification provisions are among the most operationally significant terms in any DPA. The speed and completeness of vendor breach notification directly affects Pinnacle\'s ability to assess the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and meet its own notification obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s breach notification requirements, which are in certain respects **more restrictive** than the standalone requirements of any single applicable regulation.

Pinnacle\'s internal data breach response standard, as adopted by the Board of Directors in October 2023, requires that the Company\'s Incident Response Team be activated within **four (4) hours** of receiving vendor notification of a breach or suspected breach. This internal standard drives the 24-hour vendor notification requirement described below; a vendor notification timeline of 48 hours or longer is insufficient to support Pinnacle\'s internal response protocols and downstream regulatory obligations.
**[5.1 Notification Timeline]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Vendor must notify Pinnacle of any actual or reasonably suspected breach of Personal Data, PHI, or California Personal Information within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. For purposes of this requirement, \"**discovery**\" means the first day on which the breach is known to the vendor, or the first day on which the breach, by exercising reasonable diligence, would have been known to the vendor. This definition is consistent with the HITECH Act\'s definition of discovery at 42 U.S.C. § 17382.

The 24-hour notification obligation applies regardless of whether the breach is confirmed or still under investigation. Pinnacle recognizes that a vendor\'s initial notification may be preliminary and that additional information will become available as the investigation proceeds. However, the failure to provide timely preliminary notification --- even where the full scope of the breach is not yet known --- deprives Pinnacle of the ability to initiate its own assessment and response activities.

Notification must be directed to Pinnacle\'s Chief Privacy Officer, Dr. Anand Krishnamurthy, at privacy-incidents@pinnaclehealth.com and by telephone at (512) 555-0199 (available 24/7), with a copy to the General Counsel\'s office at legal-notices@pinnaclehealth.com.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides **preliminary telephonic notification** within **four (4) hours** of discovery, followed by **written notification** within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery. The telephonic notification should include the vendor\'s initial assessment of the nature of the incident, the categories of data potentially affected, and the vendor\'s immediate containment measures. This telephonic-plus-written approach allows Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team to begin its assessment in parallel with the vendor\'s investigation.

**Fallback:** The 24-hour notification timeline is a **firm requirement**. Pinnacle will not accept timelines exceeding 24 hours for processor-to-controller notification. Negotiators should be aware that many vendor DPA templates propose **48-hour** or **72-hour** notification timelines. These proposals must be rejected and redlined to 24 hours. The following talking points may be useful in negotiations:

> • The **72-hour timeline** referenced in GDPR Article 33(1) is the *controller\'s* obligation to notify the *supervisory authority*, not the processor\'s obligation to notify the controller. GDPR Article 33(2) requires processors to notify controllers \"without undue delay after becoming aware\" of a breach, which the European Data Protection Board has interpreted as requiring notification significantly faster than 72 hours.

> • A **48-hour** processor-to-controller timeline is insufficient because it compresses Pinnacle\'s time to assess the breach, engage legal counsel, activate its incident response plan, and prepare its own regulatory notifications. Under HIPAA, Pinnacle must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery, and discovery is deemed to occur when the Business Associate notifies the Covered Entity. Under CCPA/CPRA, California\'s data breach notification statute (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.82) requires notification \"in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.\" Every hour of delay in vendor notification reduces Pinnacle\'s available response window.

> • Pinnacle\'s **24-hour standard** is consistent with market practice for healthcare data processing engagements and is required by multiple state breach notification statutes that apply to Pinnacle.
**[5.2 HIPAA-Specific Breach Notification Obligations]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must include the full HIPAA/HITECH breach notification cascade, reflecting the following obligations:

> **(a)** Vendor (as Business Associate) notifies Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) within **twenty-four (24) hours** of discovery of a breach of Unsecured PHI. This notification triggers Pinnacle\'s own assessment and notification obligations.

> **(b)** Pinnacle notifies affected individuals within **sixty (60) days** of discovery of the breach, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.404. The notification must be in writing, sent by first-class mail to the individual\'s last known address (or by email if the individual has agreed to electronic notice), and must include the elements specified in 45 CFR § 164.404(c).
> **(c)** Pinnacle notifies HHS as follows:
> • For breaches affecting **500 or more individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408.

> • For breaches affecting **fewer than 500 individuals**: notification to the HHS Secretary no later than **sixty (60) days after the end of the calendar year** in which the breach was discovered, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.408(c).

> **(d)** For breaches affecting **500 or more residents** of a state or jurisdiction, Pinnacle must notify **prominent media outlets** serving that state or jurisdiction within **sixty (60) days** of discovery, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.406.

The DPA/BAA must clearly allocate responsibility for each step of this notification cascade. While vendor (as Business Associate) is responsible for the initial notification to Pinnacle, Pinnacle (as Covered Entity) is responsible for notifications to individuals, HHS, and the media. However, vendor must provide Pinnacle with all information reasonably necessary to enable Pinnacle to fulfill its notification obligations.
**Must-have:** Vendor\'s breach notification to Pinnacle must include, at a minimum, the following information:
> \(i\) The nature of the breach, including a description of what happened and the circumstances of the unauthorized access, use, or disclosure;
> \(ii\) The types of PHI involved in the breach (e.g., names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, diagnoses, treatment information, health plan identification numbers);
> \(iii\) The identification of each individual whose PHI was, or is reasonably believed to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of the breach;
> \(iv\) A description of steps that affected individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;
> \(v\) A description of what vendor is doing to investigate the breach, mitigate harm to affected individuals, and prevent future breaches; and
> \(vi\) Contact information for the vendor\'s incident response lead, including name, title, telephone number, and email address.

**Must-have --- Late Notification Penalties:** Breach notification timelines are only meaningful if vendor faces commercial consequences for failure to comply. Pinnacle\'s preferred penalty clause is as follows:

> **Preferred position:** Vendor shall pay Pinnacle liquidated damages of **\$5,000 per day** for each day that vendor\'s breach notification is late (i.e., each day beyond the 24-hour notification deadline), with **no cap** on the total amount of liquidated damages. The parties acknowledge that the harm to Pinnacle from late notification is difficult to quantify and that this amount represents a reasonable estimate of such harm.

> **Fallback:** If the vendor proposes a counter to the liquidated damages provision, Pinnacle will accept a per-day penalty with a reasonable cap, provided that the per-day amount is **no lower than \$2,500** and the cap is **no lower than \$250,000**. Any vendor proposal below these thresholds must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park.
**[5.3 Breach Notification Content Requirements]{.underline}**
Regardless of the applicable regulatory regime, all breach notifications from vendor to Pinnacle must include the following minimum content:
> \(a\) The **nature and scope** of the breach, including a description of the incident and the systems, databases, or facilities affected;
> \(b\) The **categories and approximate number of data subjects or individuals** affected by the breach;
> \(c\) The **categories and approximate number of personal data records** affected, including the types of data elements involved;

> \(d\) The **likely consequences** of the breach for affected data subjects or individuals, including an assessment of the risk of identity theft, financial harm, reputational harm, or harm to physical safety;
> \(e\) The **measures taken or proposed** by vendor to address the breach, including containment measures, remediation steps, and measures to prevent recurrence;
> \(f\) The **identity of affected individuals** (where known), to the extent necessary for Pinnacle to fulfill its own notification obligations; and

> \(g\) **Contact information** for the vendor\'s designated incident response lead, including name, title, direct telephone number, and email address, available on a 24/7 basis for the duration of the incident response.

Vendor must provide updates to the initial notification as additional information becomes available, and must cooperate fully with Pinnacle\'s Incident Response Team throughout the investigation and remediation process.
**[Section 6: Liability and Indemnification]{.underline}**

Liability provisions are among the most heavily negotiated terms in any DPA. The allocation of financial risk between Pinnacle and its vendors must reflect the magnitude of the data at stake, the severity of potential regulatory penalties, and the operational and reputational harm that a data breach or compliance failure could cause. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required liability framework, including liability caps, carve-outs, and indemnification obligations.

Pinnacle\'s position on liability is informed by the following considerations: (i) a breach of PHI affecting Pinnacle\'s approximately 2.1 million US patients could result in HIPAA penalties of up to \$2,067,813 per violation category per calendar year, plus class action litigation exposure; (ii) a CCPA/CPRA violation could result in statutory damages of \$100 to \$750 per consumer per incident, which at 890,000 California residents represents potential exposure of \$89 million to \$667.5 million; and (iii) GDPR penalties can reach up to €20 million or 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. Against this backdrop, vendor liability caps that are a fraction of annual fees are commercially unreasonable and legally inadequate.
**[6.1 Liability Cap]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** Vendor\'s aggregate liability for all claims arising under the DPA must be no less than **two times (2x) the total annual fees** attributable to the affected data processing activity.
For reference and illustration:
**Scenario**                    **Annual Fees**         **Minimum DPA Liability Cap**
Combined US and EU engagement   \$4,200,000             \$8,400,000
US-only fees                    \$2,800,000             \$5,600,000 (for US-specific claims)
EU-only fees                    \$1,400,000             \$2,800,000 (for EU-specific claims)

Where fees are allocated by region (e.g., \$2.8 million US and \$1.4 million EU), the cap for EU-specific claims would be no less than \$2,800,000 (2 × \$1,400,000) and for US-specific claims no less than \$5,600,000 (2 × \$2,800,000).
**Must-have:** Liability must be **uncapped** for the following categories of claims:
> \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
> \(c\) **Breaches of confidentiality obligations** involving intentional or reckless conduct; and
> \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.

**Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.

**Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.

**Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.
**[6.2 Indemnification]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Vendor must indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Pinnacle, its officers, directors, employees, agents, and affiliates (including Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.) from and against all losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of litigation) arising from or related to:

> \(a\) **Third-party claims** (including claims by data subjects, consumers, patients, and healthcare providers) arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or any applicable data protection law;

> \(b\) **Regulatory fines, penalties, assessments, and enforcement costs** imposed on Pinnacle by any governmental authority (including HHS OCR, the California Attorney General, the California Privacy Protection Agency, and any EU/EEA supervisory authority) arising from or related to vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws; and

> \(c\) **Costs of breach response**, including but not limited to: costs of breach notification to affected individuals and regulatory authorities; costs of credit monitoring and identity theft protection services provided to affected individuals; costs of forensic investigation; costs of public relations and crisis communications; and costs of regulatory reporting and compliance remediation, in each case to the extent arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or applicable data protection law.

Indemnification obligations should be subject to the same uncapped/capped structure as direct liability set forth in Section 6.1 above. Specifically, indemnification for claims arising from willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional breaches of confidentiality, and regulatory fines resulting from vendor non-compliance must be uncapped. Indemnification for all other claims may be subject to the aggregate liability cap (2x annual fees), but must not be subject to any lower cap or sublimit.
Vendor\'s indemnification obligations must be in addition to, and not in limitation of, any other rights or remedies available to Pinnacle at law or in equity.
**[Section 7: CCPA / CPRA Service Provider Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section sets forth the mandatory contractual provisions that must appear in all DPAs where the vendor processes personal information of California residents on Pinnacle\'s behalf. These provisions are required to establish the vendor\'s status as a \"Service Provider\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which is essential to Pinnacle\'s compliance with the statute.
**[7.1 Service Provider Contractual Terms]{.underline}**
**Must-have:** The DPA must include the following CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag):

> **(a) Prohibition on Selling or Sharing.** Vendor is prohibited from selling (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad)) or sharing (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ah)) any personal information received from, or on behalf of, Pinnacle. This prohibition applies regardless of whether the vendor receives monetary or other valuable consideration in exchange for the personal information.

> **(b) Purpose Limitation.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle for any purpose other than performing the services specified in the DPA and the applicable MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement. Vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information for vendor\'s own business purposes, including but not limited to marketing, product development, analytics, or profiling, unless such use is expressly authorized by Pinnacle in writing and is consistent with a permissible business purpose under the CCPA/CPRA.

> **(c) Restriction to Direct Business Relationship.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle outside of the direct business relationship between Pinnacle and vendor. This means that vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information to provide services to any other client or customer of vendor, or for any purpose unrelated to the services vendor provides to Pinnacle under the DPA/MSA.

> **(d) Prohibition on Combining.** Vendor is prohibited from combining personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information that vendor receives from or on behalf of any other person or entity, or that vendor collects from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA (e.g., to detect data security incidents or protect against fraud).

> **(e) Service Provider Certification.** Vendor must include a certification, executed by an authorized representative of vendor, stating that vendor understands the restrictions set forth in subparagraphs (a) through (d) above and will comply with them. This certification is a statutory requirement under the CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and must appear in the DPA itself or in a CCPA/CPRA Addendum appended to the DPA.

> **(f) Right to Monitor Compliance.** Vendor must grant Pinnacle the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that vendor uses personal information in a manner consistent with Pinnacle\'s obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. This includes the right to conduct ongoing manual reviews, automated scans, and assessments of vendor\'s systems and practices as they relate to the processing of personal information received from Pinnacle.

> **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor agrees to cooperate with Pinnacle in responding to CCPA/CPRA consumer requests, including the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), and the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), within timelines consistent with the statute. Under the CCPA/CPRA, Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor\'s cooperation must be sufficiently prompt to allow Pinnacle to meet these deadlines.

**Fallback:** If the vendor\'s DPA template contains no CCPA/CPRA provisions whatsoever, Pinnacle will require a **standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum** appended to the DPA. The addendum must contain all of the provisions listed in subparagraphs (a) through (g) above and must be expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should use the template language provided in Appendix B as a starting point for drafting the addendum.
**[7.2 California Consumer Volume]{.underline}**

As of February 2025, Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient platform, provider network, and associated data processing activities. This volume is expected to grow as Pinnacle\'s US user base expands. All vendors with access to California resident personal information, regardless of the volume of records processed by any individual vendor, must comply with the requirements set forth in Section 7.1 above.
**[Section 8: Audit Rights]{.underline}**

Audit provisions are a cornerstone of any effective DPA. Pinnacle\'s ability to verify vendor compliance with HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR depends on having contractual audit rights that are robust enough to cover all data processing locations, including subprocessor facilities, and all relevant compliance domains. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s audit right requirements.
**[8.1 Scope of Audit Rights]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Pinnacle must have the contractual right to audit vendor\'s data processing activities, directly or through a qualified third-party auditor designated by Pinnacle. The scope of the audit right must include:

> **(a) All data center locations** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. Audit rights must not be limited to the vendor\'s primary data center; they must extend to all locations, including secondary, disaster recovery, and backup sites.

> **(b) All subprocessor facilities** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. This requirement is critical where subprocessors operate in different jurisdictions from the vendor (e.g., a US subprocessor handling EU data under a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer). Subprocessor audit coverage is essential to verifying end-to-end compliance with the data protection requirements applicable to Pinnacle\'s data.

> **(c) Vendor\'s policies, procedures, and technical controls** relevant to data protection, including but not limited to: information security policies, access control procedures, incident response plans, data classification policies, encryption configurations, and vulnerability management programs.

> **(d) Vendor\'s compliance with HIPAA Security Rule safeguards** specifically, including administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312), where vendor is a Business Associate.
**Must-have:** Audit rights must extend to subprocessor locations. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with one of the following mechanisms for subprocessor audit coverage:

467: **[Section 9: Data Return, Deletion, and Retention]{.underline}**
468: 
469: This Section addresses the provisions governing the disposition of data at the end of the vendor relationship, including the critical interplay between post-termination data deletion obligations and HIPAA\'s six-year record retention requirement. Getting these provisions right is essential to ensuring both a clean transition and ongoing regulatory compliance.
470: 
471: **[9.1 Data Return Option]{.underline}**
472: 
473: **Must-have:** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, for any reason, vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **data return option** --- that is, the right to receive a complete copy of all Personal Data, PHI, and California Personal Information processed by vendor under the DPA, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, before any deletion occurs. The data return option must be exercisable at Pinnacle\'s sole election; vendor may not condition the return of data on payment of additional fees beyond those specified in the DPA/MSA, nor may vendor require Pinnacle to waive any rights or claims as a condition of data return.
474: 
475: **Must-have:** Vendor must provide **at least thirty (30) calendar days of transition assistance** following Pinnacle\'s request for data return, during which period vendor must: (i) continue to securely host and maintain Pinnacle\'s data in accordance with all security and confidentiality obligations of the DPA; (ii) cooperate in data migration activities, including by making data available for export through secure channels and in agreed-upon formats; (iii) make relevant vendor personnel available to support the transition, including technical staff familiar with the data structures and systems involved; and (iv) refrain from deleting any Pinnacle data until Pinnacle has confirmed in writing that the data return is complete.
476: 
477: **Must-have:** Following completion of data return (or upon Pinnacle\'s written instruction to proceed directly to deletion without return), vendor must **securely delete all copies** of Pinnacle data in vendor\'s possession, custody, or control, including copies in active systems, staging environments, archives, and backup media. Pinnacle\'s playbook target is deletion within **thirty (30) calendar days** following completion of data return or receipt of Pinnacle\'s deletion instruction; the maximum acceptable deletion window is **sixty (60) calendar days**. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **written certification of deletion** signed by an authorized officer of vendor, confirming that all copies of Pinnacle data have been securely deleted using methods consistent with NIST SP 800-88 or equivalent standards.
478: 
479: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides data return in Pinnacle\'s preferred format (to be specified in the DPA or MSA), with all metadata intact and in a structure that facilitates import into Pinnacle\'s systems or a successor vendor\'s systems without material data loss or reformatting.
480: 
481: **Fallback:** If vendor insists on a longer deletion window (e.g., 90 days), this is acceptable only if: (i) the data return option is fully preserved; (ii) the 30-day transition assistance period is preserved; (iii) all security, confidentiality, and use restrictions of the DPA continue to apply to retained data throughout the extended deletion window; and (iv) vendor provides a written explanation of why 90 days is required (e.g., backup media rotation schedules).
482: 
483: **[9.2 HIPAA Record Retention]{.underline}**
484: 
485: **Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must acknowledge and account for HIPAA\'s **six (6) year record retention requirement** under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later. The categories of documentation subject to this requirement include:
486: 
487: > • The BAA itself;
488: >
489: > • Policies and procedures related to the privacy and security of PHI;
490: >
491: > • Workforce training records and training materials;
492: >
493: > • Security incident and breach response records;
494: >
495: > • Risk assessments and risk management documentation;
496: >
497: > • Access logs and audit trails related to PHI; and
498: >
499: > • Any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance with HIPAA requirements.
500: 
501: **Must-have:** The six-year HIPAA retention obligation must be **expressly reconciled** with the post-termination deletion obligation set forth in Section 9.1 above. Without an express reconciliation, the deletion obligation and the retention obligation create an internal contradiction that could result in either premature deletion of HIPAA-required records or indefinite retention of PHI without adequate contractual protections. Pinnacle\'s recommended reconciliation language is as follows:
502: 
503: > *\"Notwithstanding the deletion obligations in this Section, Processor shall retain such records as are required to comply with HIPAA record retention requirements (45 CFR § 164.530(j)) for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when such records were last in effect, whichever is later. Such retained records shall remain subject to the confidentiality, security, and use restrictions of this Agreement and the Business Associate Agreement for the duration of the retention period. Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, Processor shall securely delete all such retained records and provide Controller with written certification of deletion.\"*
504: 
505: **Red line:** Any post-termination deletion clause that does not carve out HIPAA record retention requirements is **non-compliant** and creates significant regulatory risk. A vendor that deletes HIPAA-required documentation within 30 or 60 days of termination may be in violation of 45 CFR § 164.530(j), and Pinnacle could face enforcement consequences if it cannot produce required documentation during an OCR investigation. Negotiators must ensure that the HIPAA retention carve-out is included in every DPA involving PHI. If a vendor\'s DPA template contains a blanket deletion-at-termination clause without a HIPAA carve-out, the clause must be redlined before execution. Escalate immediately if the vendor refuses to include the carve-out.
506: 
507: **[Section 10: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**
508: 
509: Governing law and dispute resolution provisions are critical in DPAs that cover both US and EU data, particularly where the vendor is a non-US entity. A DPA that applies a single non-US governing law and non-US dispute resolution forum to all disputes --- including disputes involving US PHI and California personal information --- could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to enforce its US regulatory rights and may be inconsistent with the jurisdictional framework of HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA enforcement. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required approach: a bifurcated governing law and dispute resolution structure.
510: 
511: **[10.1 Bifurcated Governing Law]{.underline}**
512: 
513: **Must-have:** DPAs covering both US and EU data must include a **bifurcated governing law clause** that applies different governing law depending on the nature of the claim and the data involved:
514: 
515: > **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.
516: >
517: > **(b) EU/EEA Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **EU/EEA data** --- including GDPR-covered personal data of EU/EEA data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **applicable EU/EEA Member State**. Where Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the contracting controller, the law of the **Netherlands** is preferred. Where the vendor is based in Germany and strongly resists Dutch law, **German law** is an acceptable alternative for EU data disputes.
518: 
519: **Nice-to-have:** Delaware law for all matters, including EU data disputes. However, this position is unlikely to be accepted by EU-based vendors and may conflict with GDPR mandatory provisions that require application of EU Member State law for certain data protection matters, including enforcement actions by supervisory authorities.
520: 
521: **Fallback:** German law for EU data disputes is acceptable, provided that Delaware law for US data disputes is preserved as a must-have. The bifurcation itself --- applying US law to US data disputes and EU law to EU data disputes --- is the critical structural requirement. Pinnacle will not accept a DPA that applies a single non-US governing law (e.g., German law) to disputes involving PHI or CCPA-covered personal information.
522: 
523: **[10.2 Dispute Resolution Forum]{.underline}**
524: 
525: **Must-have:** The DPA must include the following forum selection provisions:
526: 
527: > **(a) US Data Disputes.** The parties consent to the exclusive jurisdiction of the **United States District Court for the Western District of Texas, Austin Division**, or, where federal subject matter jurisdiction is unavailable, the **state courts of Travis County, Texas**, for all disputes arising from or related to the processing of US data. This forum selection reflects the location of Pinnacle\'s principal offices and the location of Pinnacle\'s primary US data processing operations.
528: >
529: > **(b) EU Data Disputes.** For disputes arising from or related to the processing of EU/EEA data, arbitration under recognized EU arbitration rules is acceptable. Pinnacle will accept arbitration administered by:
530: >
531: > • The **DIS** (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit / German Institution of Arbitration) Rules, seated in Germany;
532: >
533: > • The **ICC** (International Chamber of Commerce) Arbitration Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction; or
534: >
535: > • The **LCIA** (London Court of International Arbitration) Rules, seated in the relevant EU jurisdiction.
536: 
537: **Nice-to-have:** Federal court jurisdiction (Western District of Texas) for all disputes, including EU data disputes. This is unlikely to be accepted by EU vendors but should be proposed as the opening position.
538: 
539: **Fallback:** Pinnacle will accept arbitration for EU data disputes but will **NOT** accept non-US arbitration or non-US courts for disputes involving US data (PHI, CCPA-covered data, or any other US personal information). Any vendor DPA that applies a non-US governing law and/or a non-US dispute resolution forum to US data disputes must be **redlined**. Escalate to Margaret Yuen-Park and Rachel Osterfeld (Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP) if the vendor insists on a non-US forum for US data disputes.
540: 
541: **Note for negotiators:** Some vendor templates apply a single governing law (e.g., German law) and a single arbitration forum (e.g., Munich) to all disputes under the DPA, regardless of the type of data or the jurisdiction of the affected data subjects. This approach is problematic for several reasons:
542: 
543: > • HIPAA enforcement is under **US federal jurisdiction**. An arbitration clause seated in Munich may not be enforceable against an OCR subpoena or investigation, and may create practical barriers to Pinnacle\'s enforcement of its HIPAA-related contractual rights.
544: >
545: > • CCPA/CPRA enforcement is under **California jurisdiction** (California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency). A German arbitration clause may create uncertainty regarding the enforceability of CCPA-related contractual provisions.
546: >
547: > • A blanket non-US forum clause could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to seek **injunctive relief** in US courts for urgent data protection matters, such as an ongoing unauthorized disclosure of PHI.
548: 
549: The bifurcated approach recommended in this Section addresses these concerns by ensuring that US data disputes are resolved in US forums under US law, while EU data disputes are resolved in EU forums under EU law.
550: 
551: **[Section 11: International Data Transfers]{.underline}**
552: 
553: While this playbook focuses primarily on US requirements, cross-border data transfers directly affect US data and must be addressed in vendor DPA negotiations. For example, EU data may be transferred to the US for disaster recovery or support purposes, and US data may be accessed remotely by vendor personnel located in the EU or other jurisdictions. The DPA must establish clear transfer mechanisms and documentation requirements for all such scenarios.
554: 
555: **[11.1 Transfer Mechanisms]{.underline}**
556: 
557: **Must-have:** Where vendor or any subprocessor transfers personal data from the EU/EEA to a third country (including the United States), the DPA must specify the applicable lawful transfer mechanism for each transfer scenario. Acceptable transfer mechanisms include:
558: 
559: > **(a) EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021. The appropriate module must be selected for each transfer relationship:
560: >
561: > • **Module 2** (Controller-to-Processor): For transfers from Pinnacle EU B.V. (as Controller) to a vendor (as Processor) located outside the EEA;
562: >
563: > • **Module 3** (Processor-to-Subprocessor): For transfers from a vendor (as Processor) to a subprocessor located outside the EEA; and
564: >
565: > • **Module 4** (Processor-to-Controller): Where applicable, for reverse transfers.
566: >
567: > **(b) EU-US Data Privacy Framework (\"DPF\")** certification: Acceptable only if the receiving entity (vendor or subprocessor) is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities. Negotiators should verify the vendor\'s DPF certification status on the International Trade Administration\'s Data Privacy Framework List (dataprivacyframework.gov) before relying on this mechanism.
568: >
569: > **(c) Binding Corporate Rules (\"BCRs\")**: Acceptable where the vendor has approved BCRs in place that have been reviewed and approved by the competent EU supervisory authority.
570: 
571: **Must-have:** The DPA must address **all** transfer scenarios, including:
572: 
573: > • Primary data hosting and processing transfers (e.g., data stored in an EEA data center and processed by a US-based vendor);
574: >
575: > • Disaster recovery and business continuity transfers (e.g., data replicated to a US-based backup facility);
576: >
577: > • Remote access from third countries (e.g., vendor support engineers located in India, the Philippines, or the US accessing EU data from non-EEA locations); and
578: >
579: > • Subprocessor transfers (e.g., vendor engages a subprocessor in a third country to perform specific processing activities).
580: 
581: **Must-have:** Vendor must conduct and document a **Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\")** for each transfer of personal data to a third country. The TIA must assess the laws and practices of the recipient country that may affect the protection of the transferred data, including government surveillance laws, and must be made available to Pinnacle upon request. Where the TIA identifies risks that cannot be mitigated by supplementary measures, the transfer mechanism may need to be reconsidered.
582: 
583: **Must-have:** If a subprocessor is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, SCCs must be executed with the appropriate module (typically Module 3, Processor-to-Subprocessor) before any personal data is transferred to that subprocessor.
584: 
585: **Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle pre-approves the specific SCC modules for each transfer relationship during DPA negotiation, ensuring clarity and reducing the need for post-execution amendments as transfer relationships evolve.
586: 
587: **Fallback:** If vendor\'s DPA template attaches only one SCC module (which is common), Pinnacle will require the addition of all applicable modules before execution. The negotiator should assess the vendor\'s transfer relationships and subprocessor arrangements to determine which modules are required and ensure that they are included in the DPA as executed.
588: 
589: **[Section 12: Subprocessing Requirements]{.underline}**
590: 
591: Vendors frequently engage subprocessors to perform specific data processing activities on their behalf. Because Pinnacle\'s data may ultimately be processed by entities with which Pinnacle has no direct contractual relationship, the DPA must include robust subprocessor requirements that ensure end-to-end protection. This Section works in conjunction with Section 8 (Audit Rights --- subprocessor coverage) and Section 4 (HIPAA BAA --- subcontractor flow-down).
592: 
593: **[12.1 Subprocessor Obligations]{.underline}**
594: 
595: **Must-have:** Vendor must impose on each subprocessor **substantially the same** data protection obligations as those imposed on vendor under the DPA. This flow-down requirement applies to all applicable regulatory regimes, including:
596: 
597: > • **HIPAA BAA flow-down terms**: Each subprocessor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI must be bound by BAA obligations equivalent to those in vendor\'s BAA with Pinnacle (per 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
598: >
599: > • **CCPA/CPRA Service Provider restrictions**: Each subprocessor that processes California personal information must be contractually restricted from selling, sharing, combining, or using the personal information for purposes other than those specified in the agreement;
600: >
601: > • **GDPR Article 28 requirements**: Each subprocessor must be bound by a written contract that provides the same level of data protection as the vendor\'s DPA with Pinnacle (per GDPR Art. 28(4)); and
602: >
603: > • **Confidentiality obligations**: Each subprocessor must be bound by confidentiality obligations at least as protective as those in the DPA.
604: 
605: **Must-have:** Vendor remains **fully liable** for the acts and omissions of its subprocessors. The DPA must include an express statement that vendor shall be responsible for the performance of its subprocessors as if such acts or omissions were vendor\'s own. The use of subprocessors does not relieve vendor of any of its obligations under the DPA.
606: 
607: **Must-have:** The DPA must include a **current list of all authorized subprocessors**, specifying for each subprocessor:
608: 
609: > • Name and corporate entity;
610: >
611: > • Location (country and, where relevant, specific data center location);
612: >
613: > • Services provided to vendor in connection with Pinnacle\'s data; and
614: >
615: > • Description of the data processing activities performed by the subprocessor.
616: 
617: This list must be appended to the DPA as an exhibit or schedule and must be updated whenever a subprocessor is added, removed, or changed.
618: 
619: **Must-have:** Pinnacle (as Controller) must be notified of any proposed new subprocessor or change to existing subprocessors with **sufficient time to assess and object** to the change before it becomes effective. The DPA must provide Pinnacle with a meaningful objection right --- that is, the right to object to a proposed subprocessor and, if the objection is not resolved, the right to terminate the DPA without penalty.
620: 
621: **Nice-to-have:** A **thirty (30) day objection window** for new subprocessors, measured from the date of vendor\'s notification to Pinnacle. This provides Pinnacle with adequate time to assess the proposed subprocessor\'s data protection capabilities, conduct due diligence, and raise any concerns before the subprocessor begins processing Pinnacle\'s data.
622: 
623: **Fallback:** An objection window of **fourteen (14) to fifteen (15) calendar days** is acceptable and is consistent with current market norms for DPA negotiations. However, the objection window must not be shorter than fourteen (14) days, and the notification must include sufficient detail about the proposed subprocessor (including the information listed above) to enable Pinnacle to make an informed assessment.
624: 
625: **[Section 13: Security Requirements]{.underline}**
626: 
627: This Section sets forth the minimum security standards that must appear in every Pinnacle vendor DPA. These requirements apply to all vendors that process Pinnacle\'s data, regardless of the regulatory regime applicable to the data.
628: 
629: **[13.1 Technical and Organizational Measures]{.underline}**
630: 
631: **Must-have:** The DPA must reference and incorporate the following security frameworks:
632: 
633: > **(a) GDPR Article 32** --- Vendor must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons. This reference is required for all DPAs involving EU/EEA data and is good practice for all DPAs.
634: >
635: > **(b) HIPAA Security Rule categories** --- Where vendor is a Business Associate, the DPA/BAA must require implementation of:
636: >
637: > • **Administrative safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.308, including security management processes, assigned security responsibility, workforce security, information access management, security awareness and training, security incident procedures, contingency planning, evaluation, and business associate contracts;
638: >
639: > • **Physical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.310, including facility access controls, workstation use, workstation security, and device and media controls; and
640: >
641: > • **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity mechanisms, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
642: >
643: > Both the GDPR and HIPAA security frameworks must be explicitly referenced in the DPA. A DPA that references only GDPR Article 32 without addressing the HIPAA Security Rule is insufficient for vendors that process PHI.
644: 
645: **Must-have:** The DPA must require the following specific security measures:
646: 
647: > • **Encryption at rest**: Minimum AES-256 encryption for all Pinnacle data at rest, including data stored on servers, databases, storage arrays, and backup media;
648: >
649: > • **Encryption in transit**: Minimum TLS 1.2 for all data in transit, with **TLS 1.3 preferred**. Use of deprecated protocols (SSL, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) is prohibited;
650: >
651: > • **Access controls**: Role-based access controls (\"RBAC\") based on the principle of least privilege, ensuring that only authorized personnel with a legitimate business need may access Pinnacle\'s data. Access must be reviewed and recertified at least quarterly;
652: >
653: > • **Multi-factor authentication**: Required for all remote access to systems containing Pinnacle data and for all administrative or privileged access.
654: 
655: **Must-have:** Vendor must hold a current **ISO 27001 certification** or equivalent information security management system certification, and must provide **SOC 2 Type II reports** covering the relevant service at least annually. Reports and certifications must be provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request.
656: 
657: **Nice-to-have:** Annual **penetration testing** conducted by a qualified third-party firm, with a summary of findings and remediation activities provided to Pinnacle. This is market standard and should be readily achievable by any vendor with a mature security program. Vendor should also agree to implement additional security measures as reasonably requested by Pinnacle to address evolving threats, emerging vulnerabilities, or changes in applicable law or regulatory guidance.
658: 
659: **[Section 14: Data Subject / Consumer Rights Assistance]{.underline}**
660: 
661: Pinnacle has obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR to respond to requests from individuals (patients, consumers, and data subjects) exercising their data protection rights. Because vendors often hold or process the data necessary to respond to these requests, vendor cooperation is essential. This Section sets forth the requirements for vendor assistance with data subject and consumer rights requests.
662: 
663: **Must-have:** Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding to data subject and consumer rights requests under all applicable regulatory regimes, including but not limited to:
664: 
665: > **HIPAA --- Individual Access Rights.** Under 45 CFR § 164.524, individuals have the right to access their PHI. Pinnacle must provide access within **thirty (30) days** of the request, with one **thirty (30) day extension** permitted upon written notice to the individual. Vendor must cooperate with Pinnacle to identify, locate, and produce the requested PHI within a timeframe that enables Pinnacle to meet this regulatory deadline.
666: >
667: > **CCPA/CPRA --- Consumer Rights.** Under the CCPA/CPRA, California consumers have the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121). Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in fulfilling these requests, including by searching vendor\'s systems for the consumer\'s personal information, executing deletion or correction instructions, and confirming completion.
668: >
669: > **GDPR --- Data Subject Rights.** Under the GDPR, data subjects have the right of access (Art. 15), the right to rectification (Art. 16), the right to erasure (Art. 17), the right to restriction of processing (Art. 18), the right to data portability (Art. 20), and the right to object (Art. 21). Pinnacle/Pinnacle EU B.V. must respond to data subject requests within **thirty (30) days** per GDPR Art. 12(3), with a possible extension of two additional months for complex or numerous requests. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding within this timeframe.
670: 
671: **Must-have:** Vendor\'s assistance timeline must be **short enough** to allow Pinnacle to meet its own regulatory deadlines. Given the regulatory timelines above, vendor delay in responding to Pinnacle\'s requests for assistance could result in Pinnacle missing a statutory deadline, with potential enforcement consequences.
672: 
673: **Nice-to-have:** Vendor responds to Pinnacle\'s data subject/consumer rights assistance requests within **five (5) business days** of receipt. This provides Pinnacle with a meaningful buffer before its own regulatory deadlines expire.
674: 
675: **Fallback:** A response timeline of **ten (10) business days** is acceptable, provided that vendor commits to best efforts to respond sooner where Pinnacle indicates that the request is time-sensitive.
676: 
677: **[Section 15: DPA Term, Survival, and Termination Provisions]{.underline}**
678: 
679: This Section addresses the DPA\'s term, its relationship to the underlying MSA, and the critical question of which provisions survive termination and for how long.
680: 
681: **Must-have:** The DPA should be **coterminous with the MSA**. The DPA should become effective upon execution of the MSA (or, if later, upon the date the vendor first processes Pinnacle data) and should remain in effect until the MSA terminates or expires, unless terminated earlier in accordance with its terms. If the MSA is renewed or extended, the DPA should automatically renew or extend for the same period.
682: 
683: **Must-have:** The following DPA provisions must **survive termination** of the DPA and the MSA for a period sufficient to cover all applicable regulatory obligations:
684: 
685: > • **Breach notification** obligations (Section 5);
686: >
687: > • **Data return and deletion** obligations (Section 9);
688: >
689: > • **Liability and indemnification** obligations (Section 6);
690: >
691: > • **Audit rights** (Section 8), to the extent necessary to verify compliance with post-termination obligations;
692: >
693: > • **Confidentiality** obligations, for as long as vendor retains any Pinnacle data; and
694: >
695: > • **HIPAA BAA obligations**, for as long as vendor retains any PHI, and in any event for the six (6) year record retention period under 45 CFR § 164.530(j).
696: 
697: **Note on HIPAA Survival:** HIPAA requires six (6) years of record retention under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Any DPA survival period shorter than six (6) years may be insufficient for HIPAA purposes, because the termination of the DPA\'s protective provisions before the end of the retention period would leave PHI-related documentation without contractual protections. Where a vendor proposes a shorter survival period (e.g., two (2) years), Pinnacle must negotiate either:
698: 
699: > \(a\) An extension of the general DPA survival period to six (6) years; or
700: >
701: > \(b\) A carve-out providing that HIPAA-related obligations (including the BAA, security obligations, audit rights, and confidentiality obligations as they relate to PHI) survive for the full **six (6) year retention period** or for as long as vendor retains any PHI, whichever is longer, even if the general DPA survival period is shorter.
702: 
703: **Fallback:** A general DPA survival period of **two (2) to three (3) years** is acceptable for non-HIPAA obligations, provided that HIPAA obligations have a separate, longer survival as described above. The negotiator should ensure that the survival clause clearly distinguishes between the general survival period and the HIPAA-specific survival period, and that the HIPAA survival is not inadvertently overridden by the general survival provision.
704:

722: 
723: The following situations constitute red-line triggers that require **immediate escalation** to Margaret Yuen-Park, regardless of the DPA\'s tier classification:
724:
